title: Streaming-continuation adapter for legacy function signatures
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Background:
The platform supports two major invocation styles for external actions: the newer OpenAI-style tool model (declarative 'tools' with streaming partial outputs and structured responses) and a number of legacy synchronous function endpoints used by older customers and internal connectors. We are seeing increased friction when customers attempt to use streaming tool workflows against legacy functions: name mismatches, incompatible response shapes, and the assumption that tool outputs arrive atomically rather than as a stream of partial events.

Problem statement:
- Streaming tool calls (model->tool->stream back) currently cannot be proxied reliably to legacy functions that expect a single final JSON payload.
- Naming discrepancies (aliases, camelCase vs snake_case, versioned names) mean we sometimes route to the wrong backend or fail to match signatures.
- Partial outputs streamed from tool-backed providers are dropped or force the runtime to buffer until completion, defeating low-latency SLOs.
- There's no consistent telemetry to measure partial-run failures or reassembly errors.

Goal:
Provide a runtime adapter that: (1) safely maps OpenAI-style tool invocations to legacy function endpoints without requiring the backend to change, (2) supports streaming continuations by chunking/merging partial outputs into sanely structured payloads, (3) preserves structured output fidelity when possible, and (4) exposes clear fallbacks and telemetry for migration.

Design overview:
1) Invocation envelope: attach an ephemeral invocation_id to every proxied tool call. The adapter proxies incoming streaming events using that id and maintains reassembly state until finalization or timeout.
2) Chunk transport format: use newline-delimited JSON (ndjson) over an internal HTTP/2 stream to send partial events to legacy functions with a minimal schema: {invocation_id, seq, part_type, payload}. part_type can be 'stdout', 'json_partial', 'metadata', 'end'. Legacy endpoints that accept ndjson can opt-in; otherwise the adapter buffers and synthesizes a final payload.
3) Name mapping: consult alias registry (local cache + periodic backfill from canonical-toolname-registry) to translate OpenAI-style tool identifiers to legacy function names. Provide a heuristics tier: exact -> normalized -> fuzzy alias with a confidence tag in telemetry.
4) Structured output preservation: when the model emits structured output (e.g., JSON schema responses), the adapter attempts incremental JSON stitching. On malformed partials, it emits a partial-repair event and continues; if repair fails, mark invocation with 'reassembly_failed' and deliver best-effort concatenated payload to legacy function.
5) Backpressure & flow control: the adapter enforces a soft window per invocation (default 16 chunks) and uses HTTP/2 windows to protect downstream. If downstream is slower than upstream, the adapter will automatically switch to 'buffer-then-post' fallback mode to avoid head-of-line blocking.
6) Error handling and fallbacks: If the legacy function returns 415/422 for the chunked format, adapter will: (a) record a compatibility metric, (b) fall back to buffered full-payload POST, and (c) surface an advisory to the owner via console with remediation steps.

Telemetry & observability:
- New metrics: streaming_proxy.invocations, streaming_proxy.chunks_reassembled, streaming_proxy.reassembly_errors, streaming_proxy.fallbacks_to_buffer, alias_resolution.confidence{high,medium,low}.
- Per-invocation trace with invocation_id, seq counts, time-to-first-chunk, time-to-last-chunk, reassembly_duration.
- Logs include sample broken partials (redacted) and the mapped legacy name for debugging.

Migration & rollout plan:
Phase 1 (canary, 2 weeks): opt-in adapter behind runtime flag; enable for internal connectors + small set of customers. Monitor reassembly_errors and fallbacks_to_buffer.
Phase 2 (beta, 4 weeks): open adapter to broader set; provide opt-out via per-customer routing rule. Publish docs and best-practice guide for making legacy endpoints ndjson-friendly.
Phase 3 (GA): adapter enabled by default with a console toggle to enforce strict name matching. Provide a migration report helper that lists compatibility hits and suggested renames.

Testing strategy:
- Unit: ndjson chunk encoding/decoding, broken-json repair heuristics, alias lookup logic.
- Integration: run end-to-end with a mock legacy function that responds with delays, returns 422 on invalid chunks, and validates reassembled payload.
- Load: simulate high-churn streaming workloads to validate memory usage and backpressure heuristics.

Trade-offs and alternatives considered:
- Push vs pull reassembly: push (adapter streams to legacy) minimizes latency but requires downstream support. Pull (buffer then post) is simpler but increases tail latency. Chosen: hybrid with graceful fallback.
- Using gRPC streaming internally instead of ndjson: gRPC gives richer flow control but many existing legacy endpoints are HTTP-only. ndjson chosen for interoperability.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Default soft window size (16 chunks) — product input requested 8 for very latency-sensitive flows.
- How to signal partial confidence to callers (add a header vs embed in response body).
- Security review on chunked payloads (some enterprise customers require HMAC per chunk).

Deliverables:
- Adapter implementation in runtime/proxy (golang), feature flag, and unit/integration tests.
- RFC + design doc updates (Confluence).
- Console UI: per-invocation trace and migration report.
- Public docs: migration guide for legacy endpoints.

Success criteria:
- Reduce customer-reported tool->legacy integration incidents by 80% for enrolled customers.
- streaming_proxy.fallbacks_to_buffer < 5% at steady state for beta customers.
- No regression in per-request P95 latency for non-proxied invocations.
